contentHtml:
Ask any doctor what slows down a hospital day, and the answer is rarely a lack of expertise. It is usually a lack of connection: a specialist who cannot join a case discussion in time, a scan that sits on one screen while the team stands around another, or a ward round that depends on who happens to be in the room. India’s hospitals have spent the last few years building digital foundations. The next chapter is about making those foundations talk to people, and that is where connected AV and digital collaboration come in.

Where India Stands Today

The groundwork is impressive. As of August 12, 2026, India had created 96.43 crore ABHA health identities, linked more than 110 crore health records, and registered over 5.47 lakh health facilities and 10.50 lakh healthcare professionals. Few countries have built a digital health spine at this scale.

Care delivery is moving online too. eSanjeevani, India’s National Telemedicine Service, crossed 50 crore teleconsultations on 15 September 2026, across all 36 States and Union Territories. It now handles roughly 2.5 to 3 lakh consultations a day and is expanding from primary care into specialist services through select AIIMS.

Hospitals are putting money behind this shift. The CII–EY HealthTech Survey 2025 found that Indian hospitals planned to raise IT innovation budgets by 25%, directing investment towards clinical outcomes, data-driven decisions and better patient journeys. Records and consultations have gone digital. The room where clinicians actually meet, discuss and decide has been slower to catch up.

Why AV Is Moving From “Nice to Have” to Core Infrastructure

Think of how a hospital really works. A tumour board brings together a surgeon, an oncologist, a radiologist and a pathologist. A critical-care review needs the intensivist, the nephrologist and sometimes a consultant sitting in another city. A medical college hospital teaches residents while patients are being treated. Every one of these moments depends on people seeing the same information at the same time.

This is the job connected AV does well. Interactive displays let a team annotate a scan together instead of squinting at a monitor. High-quality video conferencing brings a remote specialist into a bedside discussion as if they were standing beside the bed. Unified communication tools keep messages, calls and shared documents in one place, so a decision made at 2 a.m. is not lost by morning.

The benefit is simple and very human: less waiting, fewer handovers that go wrong, and more time spent on patients rather than on chasing colleagues. For a country where specialists are concentrated in large cities, it also means expertise can travel further than any one doctor can.

The Trends Shaping Adoption

Three shifts stand out. First, hospitals are treating collaboration as a clinical need, not an IT upgrade. Industry leaders surveyed by Digital Health News describe a pivot towards enterprise-wide AI adoption, digital patient experience, interoperability and data governance as core enablers rather than IT add-ons.

Second, the smaller players are joining in. Digital health adoption is expanding beyond metropolitan corporate networks, with smaller clinics and mid-sized nursing homes increasingly adopting digital records. As these facilities connect, the demand for simple, reliable collaboration tools will follow.

Third, telemedicine has changed expectations. Once patients and doctors are comfortable with a video consultation, they expect the same quality inside the hospital too, in the OPD, the ward and the seminar room.

The Roadblocks Hospitals Still Face

None of this is effortless. The biggest hurdle is that systems often do not speak to each other. A Grant Thornton Bharat analysis notes that despite multiple digital systems, seamless interoperability across clinical, diagnostic and enterprise platforms remains limited. The same study found that 36 per cent of hospitals are very confident about data privacy and interoperability compliance.

That caution is healthy. A video call that cannot pull up the right patient record, or a display that cannot safely share a scan, creates more friction than it removes. Add legacy equipment, tight budgets, and the very real challenge of getting busy clinicians to change routines, and it becomes clear why technology alone is not the answer.

Interoperability Is the Real Unlock

This is why interoperability sits at the centre of the conversation. When AV platforms, hospital information systems and records tools are built to work together, collaboration stops being a separate activity. A doctor joins a consult, sees the patient’s history, reviews images on a shared screen and records the outcome, all in one flow.

India’s national frameworks are already nudging the market in this direction. Hospitals and digital solution companies earn cash incentives under the Digital Health Incentive Scheme for creating interoperable digital health records. Hospitals planning AV investments would do well to follow the same principle: choose open, standards-friendly systems, think about security from day one, and plan for integration rather than adding tools one at a time.

Building Hospitals That Are Ready for What’s Next

The opportunity here is practical. Start where the pain is greatest, such as multidisciplinary meetings, teleconsultation rooms, training spaces and command centres. Involve doctors and nurses early, because tools that feel natural get used and tools that feel imposed get ignored. Train teams, measure what improves, and expand from there.

Hospital modernisation has so far been about digitising what hospitals know. The next phase is about helping the people inside them work as one connected team, wherever they are. Connected AV and digital collaboration will not replace clinical judgement, but they can give that judgement the speed, context and reach it deserves. The hospitals that treat communication as core infrastructure, not an afterthought, will be the ones ready for the future of care in India.
